subheadings: 🇺🇸 United States  Mixed  data-dependent / Fed on hold
🇪🇺 European Union  Mixed  inflation spike / hike debate
🇨🇳 China  Mixed  stimulus talk / deflation persists
🇯🇵 Japan  Mixed  fiscal relief vs. yen and wage squeeze
🇦🇺 Australia  Mixed  hawkish RBA / bank strength
🇵🇱 Poland  Mixed  rating risk / defence money

Greenland and the Arctic minerals route

body: Wednesday, February 11 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: Mixed. The labour market is cooling faster than the activity data suggest. ADP showed only 22,000 private payrolls in January, job openings fell to the lowest since 2020, and January layoffs were the highest for a start to a year since 2009. Hiring slowed in December, defying the Fed’s effort to boost the labour market. Activity is firmer: the services PMI printed 53.8% and the ISM manufacturing index hit a three-year high. Cleveland Fed’s Hammack says rates could be on hold ‘for quite some time’. Markets are therefore pricing a Fed that is not in a hurry, and the labour data are the only near-term way to change that view.

Rates & Curve: The US Treasury par curve at the prior close has the 2Y at 3.45% and the 10Y at 4.16%, a 10Y−2Y spread of 71 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-10). The curve shape is moderately steep, approaching the long-run average, and the 20-observation move is bull steepening (both down, 2Y down more): the 2Y is down 9 bps and the 10Y down 3 bps, which widens the spread by 6 bps. Over five observations both yields fell 12 bps. Equities are mixed: the Dow closed at 50,188.14, up 1.92% over five sessions, while the S&P 500 at 6,941.81 is down 0.51% over 20 sessions and the Nasdaq 100 is down 2.56% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The VIX rose 2.48% in the prior session to 17.79, and the dollar index at 96.80 is down 2.08% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

New / Most Important: The January jobs report comes out on Wednesday, February 11, the first jobs print of 2026, after a shutdown delay. The White House is already lowering expectations for it. A homeland-security funding shutdown is nearing amid a stalemate. The House defeated a Republican bid to block votes on Trump’s tariffs, and a GOP revolt has opened a lane for votes that challenge them. On the Fed, Trump says Warsh can get the economy to 15% growth, Citi says he will face challenges shrinking the portfolio, and Barron’s says the bond market is already delivering him a tough lesson. Miran says the data suggest Americans are not shouldering the tariff hit. Robinhood’s revenue disappointed on the crypto slowdown and its shares fell, and the S&P 500 still cannot close above 7,000.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Trade the print, not the narrative. A soft payroll number on February 11 with the 2Y falling further extends the bull steepening: keep the front-end steepener, long 2Y against short 10Y, and avoid adding equity beta while the S&P is capped below 7,000. A firm print would steepen less and favour rate-sensitive financials, although AI-disruption fears have hit brokers and wealth managers. Keep tech underweight: the Nasdaq 100 at 25,127.64 is down 2.56% over 20 sessions, and Goldman’s Solomon calls the software selloff ‘too broad’, which is the signal that a rebound needs a catalyst.

Macro Stance: Mixed. The inflation number is the problem: a Euronews headline says euro-area inflation spiked to 3.8%, and Nagel’s remark that markets price over a 95% chance of a September hike is still the anchor. Standard Chartered sees limited odds of an October hike, so the path is front-loaded rather than rolling. ECB members remain divided on whether the inflation dip matters.

Credit & Inflation: EUR/USD at 1.1904 is up 2.03% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and the euro keeps strengthening with the dollar weak. Credit is still being extended: the ECB is widening access to euro loans, and euro-zone ministers are weighing euro stablecoins and joint debt to boost the euro’s role. Activity is tentative: German industrial recovery is still tentative despite rising exports. The STOXX 600 at 620.97 is up 1.72% over 20 sessions and the Euro Stoxx 50 at 6,047.06 is up 0.29% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Activity data are the weak link, so the bank rally has to come from capital return rather than loan growth.

New / Most Important: The European Parliament backed the digital euro and aligned with the Council on a currency that is ready both online and offline. The Bank of France governor offered a shock early resignation, and global yields eased as the French fiscal and political concerns grew. Von der Leyen is pitching a two-speed Europe ahead of a Draghi-style summit. Macron warns of renewed friction with the US and urges the EU to use a ‘Greenland moment’ to push reforms, and the European Parliament is set to approve the EU–US trade deal in two weeks.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Own euro-area banks through the upgrade: Deutsche Bank has turned bullish on European banks, and the buyback theme is intact. Hedge the euro, though: EUR/USD is up 2.03% over 20 sessions, and the September-hike pricing is what holds it up. If Standard Chartered is right that October odds are limited, the rate support fades and the euro is exposed. The trigger to watch is the next euro-area inflation print: a confirmed 3.8% keeps the ECB bid and the euro firm. Europe’s safe-haven role is also in play, with Kocher saying Europe must prepare for a greater global safe-haven role.

Macro Stance: Mixed. Beijing is promising support while the price data still show deflation. The central bank has promised financial support to boost domestic demand, and the grid programme is set at 5 trillion yuan over five years. Consumer inflation rose less than expected in January while producer deflation persisted, and the WSJ describes the same split between eased consumer inflation and continuing producer declines. The growth target is being trimmed too, so the policy message is patience rather than a stimulus surge.

PMIs & Activity: The feed carries no fresh official PMI headline with a figure. The latest hard activity read is autos: China’s auto sales fell at the fastest pace in nearly two years in January. Factory deflation eased more than forecast at the start of the year, but Reuters says China has made only a small dent in its deflation battle while the supply-demand imbalance persists. The one-line read is that the volume side is soft and the price side is only slowly turning. The Xinhua review of 2025 performance in a global frame is the official backdrop for that read.

Credit Impulse: Credit support is coming through the policy channel rather than through private borrowing. The Shenzhen government is drafting an $11.6 billion rescue package for China Vanke, which is targeted state support rather than a broad credit turn. Citi expects China’s property slump to hurt some Hong Kong banks’ 2025 earnings. The feed gives no evidence of a broad household-credit recovery. A Reuters poll shows the market expects January bank lending to rise on predictable monetary policy, which means the expected credit line is steady rather than accelerating.

Property: Property remains the drag. S&P has cut its China property sales forecast as the market slump deepens. The Vanke rescue is a rescue of one developer, not a sector fix. Shanghai’s state home-purchase pilot in three districts is still district-level, and the feed shows no national measure to match it.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The trade front is hardening on both sides. The EU is weighing a 30% ‘mega tariff’ on China-made EVs, with a French minister urging caution, while VW’s Cupra Tavascan was spared EU duties on China-made EVs. Beijing is signalling leverage: China’s Li inspected rare-earth facilities and hinted at leverage in the US rivalry. The Shanghai chip fund was boosted 11-fold, a self-reliance signal that goes with the 5-trillion-yuan grid plan.

Markets & Flows: The Hang Seng closed at 27,183.15, up 0.58% in the prior session and 1.25% over 20 sessions. The Shanghai Composite closed at 4,128.37, down 0.25% over 20 sessions. ASHR is at 34.03, down 0.9% over 20 sessions, and KWEB is down 8.90% over 20 sessions at 34.31. USD/CNY at 6.9220 is down 0.73% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Mainland investors are piling into Hong Kong-listed drug stocks, and China stocks won the most MSCI index additions in nearly three years.

New / Most Important: The yuan is at its strongest since 2023, and the UK has become the first foreign country with two Chinese-owned yuan clearing banks, a sign that offshore yuan use is institutionalising. Beijing is tightening market oversight to create a ‘slow bull’, which is the regulator’s own goal for equities. The grid and chip-fund spending are the fiscal items most likely to matter for capex.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Own the policy-backed Hong Kong names with mainland buyers and the MSCI inflows, and keep the yuan long against the dollar on reserve diversification. Keep KWEB underweight: it is down 8.90% over 20 sessions. Trigger to add: a national property measure, rather than the three-district Shanghai pilot. ⚠ Divergence: the yuan’s strength and the Hang Seng’s gain sit against KWEB down 8.90% over 20 sessions and China’s auto sales falling at the fastest pace in nearly two years.

Macro Stance: Mixed. Takaichi’s supermajority is intact, but the domestic numbers are getting harder. Real wages fell for the full year as prices advanced, Tokyo CPI came in hot, and business bankruptcies hit a 13-year high in January. The US has said it will boost security and economic cooperation with Japan after the LDP win. The Nikkei’s record and the political mandate suggest the market will give Takaichi room, but the yen will set the limit.

Activity & Currency: The Nikkei 225 closed at 57,650.54 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, up 2.28% in the prior session and 7.66% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). USD/JPY is at 156.13, down 1.17% over 20 sessions, as the yen keeps a winning streak. The yen gave back post-payrolls gains despite dollar weakness, and intervention speculation keeps moving the currency. Japan’s government debt rose to a record ¥1.34 quadrillion in 2025, and a Japan bond blowout is pushing corporate borrowers to convertibles.

New / Most Important: The Bank of Japan has quietly embarked on an ETF sale set to last a century. That is the most important structural item of the week: the central bank is shrinking its equity holdings slowly. The BoJ board nominee is to go to parliament as early as February 25. Trump’s support for Takaichi is said to mask fury over investment delays, which is a reminder that the US relationship has conditions attached.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Stay long Japanese equities on the election and fiscal trade, but size for the yen: USD/JPY at 156.13 is already 1.17% lower over 20 sessions, with intervention speculation capping it. Hedge with yen calls if the pair moves back toward 160. The trigger to change the view is the nominee’s parliamentary path toward February 25: a central-bank board pick that signals tightening supports the yen and hurts the export names. Wages are the constraint on the next policy move: real wages fell for the full year, which limits how far the central bank can tighten without hurting households.

Macro Stance: Mixed. The RBA is hawkish and the banks are booming. Governor Hauser says inflation is ‘too high’ and cannot be allowed to persist, and the deputy governor says changes to ‘three key facts’ prompted the rate rise. Commonwealth Bank posted a record first-half profit on market-share gains, while Telstra is cutting up to 650 roles. Household spending fell in December after two strong months, which is the squeeze the RBA is pricing. The deputy governor says the policy change rests on three key facts, so the policy is data-led rather than political.

Demand & Financing: AUD/USD at 0.7084 is up 5.6% over 20 sessions and 1.84% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and the S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,867.40, up 1.23% over 20 sessions and down 0.5% in the prior session. Australian dollar and yen are at levels not seen since the 80s, a sign of how far the carry has run. The government’s own spending boom is reshaping the economy, and Chalmers’ inflation claims were questioned over excluded spending. The Finance Sector Union has attacked ANZ over job cuts.

New / Most Important: A Chinese flotilla sailed to the edge of Australia’s exclusive economic zone, the chief says, a security item that sits alongside the trade fight over Chinese steel. Blackstone and Coatue have granted a $10 billion loan to an Australian AI firm. The RBA’s September hike expectations have strengthened after the February decision, so the rate path is still rising.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Own the banks on results, starting with the record CBA half, but avoid the domestic cyclicals where the RBA’s tone has not changed. Treat the Australian dollar as a carry trade with a stop: at 0.7084 it has already gained 5.6% over 20 sessions. The trigger to change the view is a second hawkish RBA signal, which would push the currency up and hurt rate-sensitive small caps. The household squeeze is the offset: the RBA is hawkish on inflation, but household spending is already falling.

Monetary & Activity: The Monetary Policy Council held rates on 4 February after a split that was only settled at the last minute, and the złoty rallied because the cut was not delivered. The NBP governor’s inflation forecast is out, and the final pension indexation is the lowest in years. Wages are rising strongly, and Polish industrial optimism is at a multi-year high.

FX & Markets: USD/PLN at 3.5332 is down 2.08% over 20 sessions and EUR/PLN at 4.2055 is down 0.04% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). EPOL is at 38.11, up 4.76% over 20 sessions, and the Beta ETF WIG20TR at 67.56 is up 3.59% over 20 sessions, after a 1.00% fall in the prior session.

Companies: KGHM at 304.60 fell 5.17% in the prior session and 10.41% over five sessions, after Trigon DM’s ‘sell’ call; the new KGHM chief has ministry targets to meet. PKN Orlen at 109.16 is up 11.42% over 20 sessions, with the shares at their highest in years on commodity profits. PKO BP at 92.56 is down 1.34% in the prior session. Dino (DNP) at 38.50 is down 8.72% over 20 sessions: management skipped a union meeting and sent lawyers, a long-serving executive is leaving, and the inspection board flagged control problems. Allegro (ALE) at 29.29 is down 9.23% over 20 sessions.

Security & New Development: Poland denies involvement in an assassination attempt on a Russian general. Poland plans an army of 500,000, and the army will gain a high-readiness reserve service. The EU ambassadors approved a €44 billion SAFE loan for Poland, and Brussels greenlit Polish defence projects under the programme. The FedEx and Advent consortium buying InPost for $9.2 billion shows foreign capital still buying Polish assets.

New / Most Important: Fitch says Poland risks a rating downgrade if its debt is not stabilised, and the warning is now part of the domestic debate. Mortgage capacity has hit a record and is close to a symbolic limit. The WIBOR case before the EU court is the domestic event that matters: Bankier’s headline dates the ruling to 12 February and asks whether it is a breakthrough for borrowers.

Playbook ✓: Mixed. Own the banks and the WIG20TR on a steady-rate path, but do not chase KGHM after its five-session slide: Trigon DM rates it a sell. Hedge the złoty against a rating decision, since a downgrade would press bonds harder than the currency. ⚠ Divergence: Orlen is at its highest in years while Fitch warns of a downgrade, and Dino is down 8.72% over 20 sessions while the WIG20TR gains. The rating path is the swing factor for the bonds, so size the position around any Fitch decision.

Narrative: The consensus is that AI is taking the software business, but the chip and hyperscaler side still captures the spend. XLK is at 142.55, down 2.89% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Goldman’s Solomon calls the software selloff ‘too broad’ and JPMorgan’s strategists say the AI fears on software are overblown, while JPMorgan says the sell-off has gone far enough.

Reported: Monday.com stock fell on a weak sales outlook amid AI-disruption fears. S&P Global shares fell on a weak 2026 forecast and AI concerns, and Barron’s says its earnings could not resolve the AI concern. Microsoft is 13.39% lower over 20 sessions at 413.27 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

EPS Upside Watch: Nvidia’s set-up is a pre-earnings preview: the stock has risen ahead of earnings, and the next catalyst is not in 2026. Nvidia is at 188.54, up 4.55% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The upside is a clean China-sales guide, which the US has said will come with guardrails.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Software is the group everyone shorts, yet hedge funds added record shorts on US stocks in the rout and JPMorgan calls the software sell-off overblown. The convention says the AI trade is consuming software; the feed says the positioning is already stretched on the short side.

Narrative: The debate is how the capex is funded. Alphabet is doubling its capital spending to $180 billion in 2026, and its dollar bond sale has drawn over $140 billion of demand. XLC is at 117.58 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and Alphabet is at 318.58, down 6.22% over five sessions and 4.0% over 20.

Reported: Spotify shares jumped on strong earnings and subscriber growth, and the record monthly user count was reported as well. Alphabet’s bond sale was increased to a total raise above $30 billion, and a 100-year bond was sold to fund the AI expansion.

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up is the funding story: the company has sold the rare 100-year bond and nearly $32 billion of bonds, so the next print is about whether the spend pays back. The communication names with clean subscriber growth, Spotify included, have the simplest upside case.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Alphabet is funding its capex through debt, which the convention reads as a balance-sheet warning. The feed shows the bond book has been oversubscribed, so the market is treating the debt as cheap and available.

Narrative: AI disruption has reached the financials. XLF is at 53.55, down 3.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The WSJ says the AI threat is widening into the financial sector, and wealth-manager stocks sank as a new AI tool sparked disruption fears.

Reported: US brokerages fell as the AI worries extended to financials, and LPL closed 8% lower. Financial-services stocks tanked after an AI announcement from Altruist, and European insurers slid after AI concerns hit US rivals.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside is limited for brokers and wealth managers until the AI-tool threat is priced. Barclays, by contrast, beat profit estimates and unveiled plans to return £15 billion to shareholders, which is the capital-return case the sector still offers.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Barclays’ capital return is the signal against the sector consensus: the bank is returning cash while the AI scare hits brokers and wealth managers. Morgan Stanley warns that the AI-led software selloff may pose a risk to the $1.5 trillion US credit market, so the financial exposure runs through credit as well as equities.

Narrative: Oil is up on the Iran risk premium while the majors cut back. Brent is at 68.80, up 7.72% over 20 sessions, and WTI at 63.96 is up 7.5% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). XLE is at 53.58, up 15.62% over 20 sessions and 3.70% over five. A third US carrier strike group is heading to the Middle East in the biggest buildup since 2003.

Reported: BP suspended its share buyback and halted buy-backs as annual profits slid, and CNBC says it did so in a fresh sign of oil-price pressure. Oil executives announced major budget cuts as prices slumped. Shell’s weakest quarterly profit in nearly five years kept buybacks steady.

EPS Upside Watch: The EPS upside is in the names that keep spending while the cash return is cut. The energy majors are cutting budgets and buybacks, so the earnings question is volume and cost, not distributions. Exxon is up 22.22% over 20 sessions at 151.59, which shows the market is paying for the oil move, not the buyback story (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The US is giving the Iran risk a military dimension: Trump has hinted at a second carrier if talks fail, and the US has issued fresh guidance to vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. The convention says the energy trade is the sanctions trade; the feed shows it is now the shipping trade as well.

Narrative: Industrials are running on defence and power. XLI is at 173.91, up 6.58% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Defence is the strongest sub-theme: Kongsberg raised its fair value estimate by 9% on record backlog, and Thales is ramping up production to meet a global defence boom.

Reported: Honda’s third-quarter profit slumped over 60% as EV restructuring bit, and Mazda is cutting costs to protect margins from tariffs. Ford’s quarterly loss was its worst since 2008 on the EV shake-up, although Ford guided for a stronger 2026.

EPS Upside Watch: Defence is the EPS upside case. Bloomberg says the US needs more missiles, not defence-stock buybacks, which is the demand signal for contractors that are investing rather than returning cash. The Kongsberg record backlog is the cleanest sign that orders are converting to revenue.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Autos are cutting cost while defence is expanding capacity. The convention says the industrial cycle is led by capex in power and factories; the feed shows the marginal growth is in defence orders, with autos in restructuring.

Narrative: Discretionary is split between brand winners and the rest. XLY is at 118.33, down 4.97% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). December retail sales stalled and came in flat, well short of estimates, and the FT says the US consumer is slowing.

Reported: Mattel shares dropped 28% after holiday sales sputtered, and Lyft fell 15% on disappointing fourth-quarter results and rider numbers. Kering jumped 12% as a new CEO mapped a revival and sales beat estimates. Spotify’s shares jumped on strong earnings.

EPS Upside Watch: Brands that re-rate on a new plan have the upside. Kering’s jump on a new CEO’s plan is the example. Dollar Tree is going after richer shoppers, which is a trade-up signal for the value channel rather than a consumer-stress signal.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail sales were flat but the value channel is trading up. The convention reads flat sales as weak demand for everything; the feed shows the mix is shifting, with Dollar Tree pursuing richer shoppers.

Narrative: Staples are still the defensive winner. XLP is at 87.15, up 8.69% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and Walmart is up 7.4% over 20 sessions at 126.70. The group is what investors buy when they want quality over growth, and Yahoo Finance’s headline says consumer staples are massively outperforming the market.

Reported: Coca-Cola missed revenue estimates and forecast modest growth amid demand concerns. CVS beat quarterly estimates and reaffirmed its profit outlook as its turnaround took effect, although the stock fell after the beat.

EPS Upside Watch: The EPS upside is in the names with a turnaround and a reaffirmed outlook. CVS shows the market will not reward a beat unless the guide moves. Coca-Cola’s revenue miss means the bar is lower for the next print.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The defensive rally is happening while the rate path is steepening: the 2Y is down 9 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-10), which argues for a staples rally that does not depend on falling yields. The convention is that staples follow the bond market; here they are following the quality bid.

Narrative: Health care is trading on guidance and on the GLP-1 trade. XLV is at 155.33 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Seeking Alpha has downgraded Hims & Hers, calling the GLP-1 trade ‘just got real’, and the category leader is still priced for the pricing pressure: Eli Lilly is down 5.18% over 20 sessions at 1,025.00.

Reported: CVS beat and reaffirmed its profit outlook, but the stock fell after the beat. CSL shares plunged to an eight-year low after a CEO departure and weak earnings. Cardinal Health jumped after its earnings, and Boston Scientific beat and became the worst S&P 500 stock that day, the same split between beats and reactions.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside case is the turnaround with a reaffirmed guide. CVS has a turnaround and a reaffirmed profit outlook, which is the cleanest set-up in the group, even though the first reaction was negative.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention says a beat with a reaffirmed guide is good news; the feed shows CVS falling after the beat. The market is discounting the durability of the turnaround, not the quarter.

Narrative: Materials are the gold and copper trade. XLB is at 52.91, up 9.05% over 20 sessions and 4.36% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). BNP says gold could hit $6,000 an ounce as the rally ‘makes sense’, and gold is at 5,031.00, up 9.02% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

Reported: Barrick’s earnings were very strong, driven by the gold bull market. Zijin Mining raised its 2028 gold output target on record prices. Anglo American cut its 2027 copper guidance as production declines.

EPS Upside Watch: The gold miners are the leveraged upside. Newmont is at 121.53, up 7.59% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Goldman says governments are hoarding commodities beyond gold, which adds a policy bid to base metals.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Copper and aluminium dipped as gains peter out before China’s holiday break, while Goldman says governments are hoarding commodities beyond gold. The convention reads copper as a China growth gauge; here it is an AI-grid asset, and today’s dip is a Chinese-demand story, not a growth signal.

Narrative: REITs have rallied on lower mortgage rates. XLRE is at 42.84, up 5.47% over 20 sessions and 4.97% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Mortgage rates are under 6% for now, and homeowners are staying put, which keeps turnover low.

Reported: Prime US REIT reported a higher distribution per unit as it lifted its payout ratio. Starhill Global REIT’s manager CEO is retiring. Boustead Singapore has been given a nod to list a REIT and to divest 15 properties.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside depends on turnover. Homeowners holding onto their houses for a record-long stretch means the transaction line is still weak, and the payout ratio story is the one visible catalyst in the feed.

⚡ Breaking Convention: REITs are outperforming while the 10-year moved little: the 10Y is down 3 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-10). The convention says REITs follow the long end; here they are following the mortgage-rate and yield-carry trade.

Narrative: Utilities are the power-demand proxy, and the power is being sold to data centres. XLU is at 44.20, up 3.80% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The White House is seeking data-centre agreements amid energy price spikes, and data centres can tap batteries and microgrids for faster interconnection.

Reported: Vistra jumped 4.33% in the prior session and is up 4.31% over five sessions, while Constellation is down 19.27% over 20 sessions at 271.14 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). NextEra is up 11.97% over 20 sessions at 90.83.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside is in the regulated names that are raising capex and have a data-centre pipeline. The data-centre cost report for Illinois shows ratepayer pressure, which is the risk for the regulated models.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Merchant power is recovering in the short term while the regulated utilities lead the 20-session move. The convention says the producer and the regulated model move together; the feed shows the merchant-power trade is a five-session bounce, not a trend.

Narrative: European autos are in a structural squeeze. The iShares auto ETF (SXAP tracker) is at 45.73, down 1.66% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Stellantis is seeking to exit its battery venture with Samsung as EV losses mount, and Germany’s auto industry is in ‘crisis’ as investment and jobs move abroad.

Reported: Stellantis stock dropped 24% after its earnings, and the dividend went with it. Volvo Cars fell over 22% in its worst trading day ever. Honda’s profit slump shows the same EV-restructuring squeeze in Asia.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside is in the German premium names that have already reset. Bankers have started work on €6.5 billion of debt for VW’s Everllence unit, which is a financing event rather than a profit one. Stellantis is 24.6% lower over five sessions at 7.48 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

⚡ Breaking Convention: VW is up 3.62% in the prior session at 104.55, and Cupra Tavascan was spared EU duties on China-made EVs. The convention says Chinese EV pressure is the auto sector’s threat; the feed shows Western brands can still win access to the EU market.

Narrative: Semiconductors are the AI supply-chain winner. SOXX is at 351.43, up 6.38% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and SMH is at 404.76, up 3.61%. TSMC’s board approved a $45 billion spending package for new fabs, and TSMC stock hit a record high.

Reported: Memory makers are set to earn $551 billion from the AI boom, twice as much as the contract chip manufacturers. Micron has fallen 11.01% over five sessions at 373.25, but it is up 7.92% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Cisco unveiled a new AI networking chip that takes on Broadcom and Nvidia.

EPS Upside Watch: Memory is the upside. Deutsche Bank says Micron can hit $500, and the memory squeeze is wreaking havoc in markets with more to come. The EPS upside is in the names whose pricing tracks the squeeze, which is why memory has become the group’s second leg.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Taiwan says it is ‘impossible’ to move 40% of chip capacity to the US, which cuts against the Washington relocation goal. The convention says US tariff pressure pulls the supply chain home; the feed says Taiwan will not give up the capacity it has.

Rewarded: Capital return and clean growth were rewarded. Spotify jumped on strong earnings and subscriber growth, and Kering jumped 12% as a new CEO mapped a revival. Barclays beat profit estimates and plans to return £15 billion to investors, with annual profit up 13%. CVS beat and reaffirmed its profit outlook, although the stock fell.

Punished: Guidance cuts and AI worries were punished. Mattel shares dropped 28% after holiday sales sputtered, Lyft fell 15% on disappointing results and rider numbers, and Astera Labs fell 10% as revenue came up short. S&P Global shares fell on a weak 2026 forecast and AI concerns, and Coca-Cola missed revenue estimates.

Pattern: The market is paying for capital return and for revenue that is not exposed to AI disruption. CVS’s beat with a reaffirmed guide still fell, which says the market is discounting the turnaround. S&P Global’s earnings could not resolve the AI concern. The rule from the last two weeks holds: the forward line and the AI exposure matter more than the headline beat.

Attention into EPS: Nvidia reports next and has risen ahead of the print. JPMorgan cut its Coinbase price target to $290 ahead of earnings, so the crypto-linked names are the next test of the trading-volume thesis. Ford’s worst quarterly loss since 2008 was followed by a 2026 guide for a stronger year. Robinhood’s print is the retail-broker test of the same question.

Playbook: Own the names with capital return and a guide that is not hit by AI disruption, such as Barclays and Spotify. Avoid beats with an AI-exposed forward line, where the CVS reaction and the S&P Global reaction show the market is not paying. The trigger to change the rule is a cluster of AI-exposed beats that rise on the day; until then the discount holds. Robinhood shows the cost of a crypto-exposed quarter: revenue disappointed and the shares fell.

Attention Gap: The Bank of Japan has quietly embarked on an ETF sale set to last a century, which is a structural seller of Japanese equities that most coverage is missing. The Japanese bond market is also being squeezed, with corporate borrowers moving to convertibles and the government debt at a record ¥1.34 quadrillion. Japanese yields and the yen are linked through that funding, so the bond sell-off matters for the equity case as well.

Exposure & Risk: Japanese equity ETFs and the largest banks, which benefit from higher yields, and the yen as a funding currency. The risk is the seller: a slow ETF sale can be read as an overhang on the Nikkei at 57,650.54, which is up 7.66% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Corporate borrowers moving to convertibles shows the bond market pushing firms toward equity-linked debt, a supply signal for equities too.

Trigger to Watch: The BoJ board nominee going to parliament as early as February 25 and any update on the ETF sale pace. A nominee who signals a faster normalisation would turn the ETF overhang into a consensus short.

Attention Gap: Coverage of the software selloff has been about equities. The credit exposure is less visible: Morgan Stanley warns the AI-led software selloff may pose a risk to a $1.5 trillion US credit market, and bond dealers are pushing up private-credit fund trading costs. The sector’s leaders say the fears are overblown. That gap between the managers and the bond dealers is what the theme trades on.

Exposure & Risk: Listed private-credit managers and business-development companies, along with the leveraged-loan funds that hold software borrowers. High yield is not yet showing it: HYG at 80.84 is down 0.25% over 20 sessions and LQD at 110.82 is up 0.28% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The risk is a redemption spiral in semi-liquid vehicles.

Trigger to Watch: A redemption gate or a write-down at a listed credit fund. The FT’s ‘will software eat the creditors?’ question is the test; a single gated fund would make the theme consensus within a week. Goldman’s Solomon thinks the software selloff is too broad, so a credit event would test whether the sell-off has overshot.

Attention Gap: Greenland is a geopolitical story in the coverage, and the minerals story is underweighted. Greenland’s ice melt is opening sea routes for critical minerals, and Macron wants the EU to use a ‘Greenland moment’ to push reforms. The coverage is about the tariffs and the consulates, not the supply. Denmark and Greenland are still negotiating with Washington, so the minerals angle is the least crowded part of the story.

Exposure & Risk: Critical-minerals developers and the Canadian and Australian juniors with Arctic or Nordic projects; the rare-earth price is already at record highs. The risk is that the Arctic route is a decade-long project, and the US–Denmark talks may not conclude.

Trigger to Watch: A formal EU or US minerals-financing package that names Greenland projects. The US critical-minerals bloc proposal is the existing framework, and a named Arctic project in it would move the theme. Until then the ice-melt route is a long-dated option rather than a trade.

Attention Gap: Poland’s defence build-out is covered as a security story. The EU has approved a €44 billion SAFE loan for Poland and greenlit Polish defence projects, but the market focus is on the rate and the zloty. The financing is the unpriced part. The security headlines are well covered; the financing and the IPO pipeline are not.

Exposure & Risk: Polish defence and drone IPO candidates, and the banks that fund the state; WB Electronics has eyed a Warsaw IPO. The risk is that the rating warning makes the financing more expensive and the IPO window narrower. The Polish banks that fund the state are the second-order exposure, and mortgage capacity hitting a record shows household credit is still expanding.

Trigger to Watch: The first SAFE-funded contract award or a Warsaw defence IPO filing. Either would turn the theme from a security story into a capital-markets one, and the Fitch decision would test the financing cost.

Market Context: Bitcoin closed at 68,793.96 on the prior completed daily close, 2026-02-10, down 23.03% over 20 sessions and up 9.72% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Ether is at 2,019.50, down 32.21% over 20 sessions, and Solana at 82.92 is down 35.91%. IBIT is at 38.97, down 24.87% over 20 sessions, and Coinbase is at 162.51, down 33.12%. Bitcoin fell to $69,000 as the market showed ‘early stages of bottoming’, and a US bitcoin ETF back-to-back inflow streak came for the first time in a month. Miners are under strain too, with mining difficulty dropping by the most since 2021 as they capitulate.

New / Most Important: Michael Saylor says Strategy will refinance its debt rather than sell bitcoin, while a bitcoin-backed bond sale was hit by the crypto turbulence. MicroStrategy is down $4.5 billion on its $54 billion bitcoin investment. Hong Kong is proceeding with stablecoin plans despite Beijing’s reservations, and South Korea’s watchdog wants tougher rules after the $40 billion bitcoin mistake. Retail is leaving: South Koreans are bailing on crypto as retail traders bemoan losses.

Playbook: Mixed. The 9.72% five-session bounce is the first real sign of demand, but the 20-session losses are large. Keep the high-beta names (COIN, MSTR) underweight until the ETF inflows persist, and keep ether underweight against bitcoin given the 32.21% 20-session drop. A bitcoin close back above $70,000 with two more inflow days would argue for a re-entry; a close below $69,000 puts the early-bottoming call in question. Ether needs its own test: it is up 10.86% over five sessions but down 32.21% over 20, so the relative trade is still to avoid it.

Global Liquidity: The central bank story is shrinking balance sheets and the policy-rate hold. The Bank of Japan has embarked on an ETF sale, and the BoJ nominee is headed for parliament. In the US, Hammack says the rate path can stay on hold for quite some time and Warsh is being asked to shrink the portfolio, while the Fed-Treasury accord debate has stirred the $30 trillion bond market. Beijing has promised financial support to boost domestic demand, and the ECB is widening access to euro loans. In Asia, the yuan story rests on plumbing: the UK’s two Chinese-owned yuan clearing banks are the example.

Rates & Dollar: The 2-year is at 3.45% and the 10-year at 4.16% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-10), with the spread at 71 bps and bull steepening over 20 observations. The dollar index at 96.80 is down 2.08% over 20 sessions and EUR/USD at 1.1904 is up 2.03% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The Commerce Secretary says the dollar is at a ‘more natural’ level for trade, and the dollar weakened after dour US data as the yen kept its winning streak. TLT is at 88.53, up 0.98% over 20 sessions, and IEF at 96.51 is up 0.34%. The steepening is a term-premium story: the long end is not rallying as much as the front end, which argues against extending duration on a payroll miss alone.

Credit Check: Private credit is the pressure point. Morgan Stanley sees a $1.5 trillion US credit market at risk from the software selloff, and bond dealers are pushing up private-credit trading costs. Investment-grade issuance is wide open: Alphabet sold almost $32 billion of bonds, drawing over $140 billion of demand. HYG at 80.84 and LQD at 110.82 are flat over 20 sessions, so public credit has not repriced yet (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). Japanese convertible issuance is the other corner of the credit market, where corporate borrowers are moving to equity-linked paper.

Equity & Fund Flows: Money is rotating away from the US tech core. Foreign stock markets are beating the US, and Wall Street’s anything-but-tech trade is shaking up the US market. US stock turnover topped $1 trillion a day. Hedge funds added record shorts on US stocks in the rout. India’s gold ETF inflows topped its equity mutual funds for the first time.

Portfolio Implication: Hold the US curve as a steepener, not a duration bet, into the Wednesday payroll print. Keep tech underweight and the software-credit exposure small. Favour the flows that are rotating: European banks, the Hong Kong names with mainland buyers, and the Japanese fiscal trade with yen hedges. The trigger to change the stance is US equity inflows turning positive while the dollar index holds below 96.80 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). For emerging markets the carry is also open: Brazil tapped global debt markets after its busiest year in decades.

What Is Priced: The January jobs report is out on February 11, after a shutdown delay, and the White House has been lowering expectations ahead of it. ADP showed just 22,000 private payrolls, and CNN calls it a possible doozy. The 2Y is already down 9 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-10), so a soft print is partly priced. The payroll number is also a test of the White House’s own expectations, so a miss would be read as a policy failure rather than a data blip.

Conditional Expression: If payrolls are weak and the 2Y falls further, the steepener pays and the Russell 2000 at 2,679.77, up 1.67% over 20 sessions, is the cyclical beneficiary (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). If payrolls are firm and the 2Y lifts back toward its February level, cut the steepener, reduce small caps and keep the dollar bid. Either outcome is a bond trade first and an equity trade second.

Risk: The first clean print after a shutdown delay can move on revisions and seasonal noise rather than the trend. The homeland-security shutdown is nearing, which would delay the next release again and leave the market trading on unofficial data. The House defeat of a GOP bid to block the tariff votes keeps the tariff story live as a separate political risk to the data.

What Is Priced: Markets price over 95% for a September hike, while Standard Chartered sees limited odds of an October hike. The inflation print is the trigger: a Euronews headline says euro-area inflation spiked to 3.8%. The ECB has signalled it can wait, and the Governing Council is split. Euro strength is the other input the ECB is watching.

Conditional Expression: If the next print confirms the spike and the September hike stays priced, the euro is supported and European banks gain through net interest margin, so keep the bank overweight. If the hike is pushed out, the euro gives back its gain against the dollar, and the STOXX 600 at 620.97 loses its rate-sensitive leg (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

Risk: A hike that is priced too early damages the export-heavy DAX, which is down 1.70% over 20 sessions at 24,987.85 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The Bank of France shock resignation adds a governance risk to the ECB story. A hike that is out of step with a Fed that is on hold would widen the policy gap.

What Is Priced: Oil is pricing a standoff with a diplomatic option. Trump hinted at a second carrier if talks fail while Iran and the US near talks, and a third carrier strike group is heading to the Middle East in the biggest buildup since 2003. The US has issued fresh guidance to vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent is at 68.80, up 7.72% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

Conditional Expression: If talks progress and sanctions ease, Brent gives back part of its 7.72% gain and the energy names lag, while airlines and the consumer benefit. If talks fail and the carriers are used, Brent moves up faster than the sanctions headlines imply. Trade the energy-versus-airline spread on the outcome, not on the headline.

Risk: The shipping risk is the one that moves oil fastest. Five scenarios for Iran and their oil impact are already being mapped, and the US has taken a harder line on Iran’s oil network. Venezuelan supply is the offset: the EIA says output could return to its pre-blockade level by mid-2026, which caps the upside if the Iran talks succeed.

What Is Priced: The EU–US trade deal is set for a European Parliament approval in two weeks, and the US House has defeated a Republican bid to block votes on Trump’s tariffs. A GOP revolt has opened a lane for votes challenging the tariffs. The market is pricing a tariff regime that may be more contested than the administration wants. The EU is also moving to ban all Russian crypto transactions, a sign that European rule-making runs on its own timetable.

Conditional Expression: If the Parliament approves the deal and the tariff votes fail, the EU exporters and German autos re-rate, and the dollar gains against the euro. If the tariff votes pass, the autos and the chip exporters take a hit, and the Taiwanese supply story faces more pressure. Trade the autos and semis on the vote count, not on the headline tariff rate.

Risk: A tariff reversal can be more disruptive than a tariff. The EU’s own mega-tariff case on China EVs shows how quickly trade lines are moving. The risk is a second wave of tariffs that closes the deal before it is ratified.

Catalyst & Thesis: Nvidia’s next print is the catalyst, and the stock has risen into it, with a preview that says it is ready to impress. The new overhang is US policy: Lutnick says Nvidia must live with guardrails around its AI chip sales to China. The thesis is that demand is intact and the China piece is smaller than the bears claim.

Price Hurdle & Risk: NVDA closed at 188.54 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, up 4.55% over five sessions and 1.95% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The hurdle is the stock’s modest 1.95% gain over 20 sessions, and a guide that does not raise China expectations would leave the stock flat. Nvidia is also up 4.55% over five sessions, so part of the set-up is already priced (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10).

Trade Expression: Buy the shares before the print only on a dip toward the five-session low, or use a call spread into the print with the upper strike above the pre-print level. Invalidate if the China guardrails expand to the data-centre business, since that would cut the volume thesis. Watch the next Nvidia guide for the China line first; that is where the policy risk shows up.

Catalyst & Thesis: Memory makers are set to earn $551 billion from the AI boom, and the memory squeeze is wreaking havoc in markets with more to come. Deutsche Bank says Micron can hit $500. The catalyst is the pricing renewal in the memory contract market, which the squeeze is driving. The squeeze is broad enough to reach the Apple supply chain, with rising memory costs in focus.

Price Hurdle & Risk: MU closed at 373.25 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, down 11.01% over five sessions and up 7.92% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The risk is Samsung’s new memory chip, which Barron’s calls bad news for Micron, and the Nvidia-chip fear.

Trade Expression: Buy on the five-session weakness, with the trade sized for a 500 target. Invalidate on a Samsung capacity increase that breaks the contract pricing, or a Micron guide that cuts the squeeze premium. The Samsung product news is the first test.

Catalyst & Thesis: Alphabet is doubling its capital spending to $180 billion in 2026, and it sold a 100-year bond to fund the AI build-out. The debt book drew strong demand. The catalyst is whether the spend returns cash, which the next guide must show. The 100-year bond is the market’s signal that funding is not the constraint.

Price Hurdle & Risk: GOOGL closed at 318.58 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, down 6.22% over five sessions and 4.0% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The risk is that the capex doubles again and the market sells the spend, as it did on the earlier beat.

Trade Expression: Neutral into the spend: buy the shares on a pullback toward the five-session low, and pair against the software basket if the AI-disruption trade continues. Invalidate if the next guide cuts margin or the bond book weakens. Watch for a second bond deal that draws weaker demand than the $140 billion seen in the bond book.

Catalyst & Thesis: The White House is seeking data-centre agreements amid energy price spikes, and the market is now pricing the power that data centres will need. Vistra is up 4.33% in the prior session at 159.60 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), and the Illinois data-centre cost report is the ratepayer risk. Data centres can also use batteries and microgrids to speed interconnection, which could ease the grid bottleneck for producers.

Price Hurdle & Risk: VST closed at 159.60 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, up 4.31% over five sessions and down 7.52% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The hurdle is the 20-session loss, which the stock has not recovered. The risk is a regulatory push to cap data-centre power costs.

Trade Expression: Buy the shares on the five-session strength, or buy a call spread into any data-centre contract announcement. Invalidate if the White House agreements cap the price the producers can earn. The Illinois ratepayer report is the first sign of a political cap.

Catalyst & Thesis: Stellantis is seeking to exit its battery venture with Samsung as EV losses mount. The thesis is that the EV write-downs are not finished, and that the dividend cut after the earnings drop was the first of more capital-return cuts.

Price Hurdle & Risk: STLA closed at 7.48 on the prior close, 2026-02-10, up 2.33% in the prior session and down 24.6% over five sessions and 28.42% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10). The risk is a short squeeze on any restructuring headline, given how far the shares have fallen.
Trade Expression: Buy puts or a put spread into the next restructuring news. Invalidate on a credible EV-plan reset that stabilises the shares above the five-session range.

Catalyst & Thesis: AppLovin rose ahead of its earnings on a retraction and short covering, which is a squeeze that has run ahead of the fundamentals. The thesis is that the print will not match the move, and that short-covering demand fades once the report is out.

Price Hurdle & Risk: AppLovin is not in the market card, so no price is given. The risk is that the squeeze continues if the print beats and the shorts keep covering, and that the stock trades on sentiment rather than the number.

Trade Expression: Short only with a defined stop above the pre-earnings high, or buy puts through the print. Invalidate if the guide is raised and the shorts cover into the print without a fade. The retraction is the reason for the move, so the shorts will test the stock again if the print is weak.

Observed Attention: Yahoo Finance asks whether GameStop is priced differently after recent meme-stock attention, and Business Insider reports Michael Burry’s pick for the next Warren Buffett is GameStop’s Ryan Cohen. Retail is following the Cohen narrative as the meme names come back into the feed. The meme-stock scorecard is the retail talking point.

Motivation & Bias: The bias is the Cohen-as-capital-allocator story: retail reads a famous name as a reason to buy, and the meme attention is treated as a signal rather than as volatility. Ten-year meme returns are the retail scorecard.

Instrument & Risk: Shares and short-dated calls. The risk is that the attention is a headline effect, and meme names reverse quickly once a Cohen comment fades. No card price is given for GME. The Cohen story is the only catalyst in the feed, so size the position for a headline reversal.

Observed Attention: Seeking Alpha’s downgrade headline says ‘the GLP-1 trade just got real’, which is a retail-favourite story about cheap access to weight-loss drugs. The attention is on the rating change rather than the earnings. Retail forums focus on the downgrade’s reasoning rather than the company’s numbers, which is why the story travels faster than the fundamentals.

Motivation & Bias: Retail buyers treat the GLP-1 price war as a consumer-access story. The bias is that the drug makers will keep losing price while the telehealth channel wins, and Eli Lilly is down 5.18% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-10), which supports that reading.

Instrument & Risk: Shares and options. The risk is a downgrade cascade if the pricing war moves to the telehealth channel. No card price is given for HIMS. The stock is the most direct way to trade the GLP-1 price debate, so size it as a sentiment instrument.

Observed Attention: Robinhood’s quarterly revenue disappointed on the crypto slowdown and its shares fell, and a Robinhood prediction-market lift was reported despite the cooling crypto business. Retail sees the broker as the proxy for its own activity. The WSJ headline frames the prediction-market business as a lift, so the broker is being valued as a platform rather than a brokerage.

Motivation & Bias: The bias is that the prediction-market business is the next growth engine, a view that the feed supports with the WSJ headline. Retail under-weights the crypto dependence that the earnings miss exposed.

Instrument & Risk: Shares. The risk is that the crypto slowdown continues into the next quarter, and the prediction-market story is smaller than the crypto line it is meant to replace. No card price is given for HOOD. The prediction-market business is the bull case the company is selling, so the next print will test whether it offsets the crypto decline.

Observed Attention: The official Trump meme coin and WLFI led losses after a World Liberty Financial probe, and the Trump meme coin is down 96% as bitcoin and meme coins slid. Retail is watching the political-token story rather than the fundamentals. The probe headline is the driver, so the attention will follow the legal news rather than the token economics.

Motivation & Bias: The bias is that the political link keeps a floor under the token, while the 96% drawdown suggests the floor is not there. Retail that bought on the political story is now trading the probe headlines.

Instrument & Risk: Tokens, with no listed instrument. The risk is liquidity and the probe outcome; the token has no earnings and no card price, so the exposure is binary. Retail should treat any new probe headline as a reason to cut rather than to average down.

Market data: Yahoo Finance, prior completed sessions; Treasury curve: US Treasury daily par yields. Changes are price changes, not total returns. Currency sessions follow exchange-local dates; crypto observations include weekends.
